title: Your Company’s Knowledge Becomes Someone Else’s Advantage
summary: Every prompt your team writes can carry your company’s edge: pricing limits, negotiation tactics, and hard-won judgment. Learn where that knowledge goes when employees use external AI tools, and how private deployment and ownership of your model and harness keep it working for you, not someone else.
body_markdown:
# **Your Company’s Knowledge Becomes Someone Else’s Advantage**


Enterprise AI conversations often focus on what a model can do. A more consequential question is what an organization gives it in order to get useful results. Internal data, carefully developed prompts, and the workflows surrounding them can contain the knowledge that differentiates a business. Deciding where that knowledge goes should be part of the AI strategy from the beginning.


In March 2025, an Australian government contractor uploaded sensitive personal information belonging to 2,031 people into ChatGPT. In September 2026, Anthropic reported that DeepSeek had secretly forwarded a technology company's confidential AI program specifications, organizational structure, and strategic objectives to Claude without the company's knowledge. Neither incident required a sophisticated cyberattack—just employees using AI to do their jobs, unaware of where their organization's sensitive information could end up.


The uncertainty nevertheless brought a familiar enterprise concern into focus. When employees use external AI tools to work through valuable internal problems, how clearly does the organization understand what happens to the information they share?


## **The concern begins with ordinary work**


An employee does not need to upload an entire company database to disclose something valuable. As recently as July 2026, security researchers discovered that xAI’s Grok Build coding assistant was silently uploading developers’ entire code repositories, including proprietary source code and sensitive credentials, to company-controlled cloud storage. The transfers occurred even when users explicitly instructed the tool not to access certain files, raising serious concerns about how much company information AI tools collect without users’ knowledge.


A developer may share proprietary code to resolve a bug. A sales leader may provide customer history and pricing flexibility to prepare a negotiation. An operations team may describe the exceptions that make its internal process work.


In each case, the employee is trying to get a better answer. The information that makes the answer useful may also be information the organization would prefer to keep private.


[The Information](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/anthropic-data-fears-prompt-nvidia-palantir-booz-allen-restrict-model-use) reported that Palantir had demanded irrevocable zero-data-retention commitments from Anthropic, while Nvidia limited its use of Anthropic’s models to less-sensitive tasks. Booz Allen Hamilton had prohibited employees from using Anthropic’s commercial AI for proprietary cybersecurity work.


The report connected customer concerns to Anthropic’s policy change allowing 30-day retention of usage logs for security purposes. These responses reflected concerns about control over proprietary information.


These examples illustrate why the issue cannot be reduced to employee intent. Someone can be doing useful work and still send information through a channel the company has not approved: that channel can be as simple and quick as a single prompt.


## **The prompt can contain the business advantage**


To get useful answers from AI, employees often need to explain how their company works. Those instructions can reveal internal strategies, decision criteria, and hard-earned expertise: even when no confidential document is attached. The obvious concern is the document attached to a conversation. The less obvious concern is the instruction written above it: your prompt.


Consider a sales team asking AI to help negotiate a major contract. To get a useful recommendation, your employee shares the company’s minimum acceptable price, the concessions it will make to win the account, and how it responds when a competitor undercuts its offer. The prompt now contains a negotiation playbook the company would never knowingly hand to the other side.


Removing the customer’s name does not remove the value of knowing how far your company is willing to bend.


A similar pattern applies to pricing, research, customer support, and software development. The workflow can contain years of accumulated judgment: what to look for, what to ignore, and what a good result should look like.


From a business perspective, removing identifying details does not necessarily remove the commercially valuable method. Organizations should therefore evaluate prompts, examples, and feedback alongside the underlying documents when deciding how their employees utilize LLM technology.


The question is whether the company is retaining control over the knowledge it is teaching the system to use.


## **A provider’s name does not tell you which rules apply**


There is an important distinction between concern about data use and evidence that a provider is using enterprise information for training.


OpenAI states that it does not train on data from ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, or its API by default. Its policy for individual services allows content to be used for training, with options to opt out. Those are materially different arrangements, even when employees think of both as simply using ChatGPT.


The distinction matters when employees use personal AI subscriptions for work. Shadow AI creates risk when employees turn to personal AI accounts instead of company-approved tools. Whether out of convenience or dissatisfaction with the tools provided, employees may unknowingly expose proprietary information to services with weaker data protections. Unlike enterprise plans, some consumer AI subscriptions allow conversations, uploaded documents, and coding sessions to be used for model training. This creates a gap in company oversight, where sensitive business information can leave the organization without its knowledge or approval.


The operational challenge is keeping those distinctions clear across the organization.


A company may have an approved enterprise workspace while employees also use personal subscriptions, coding assistants, and AI features inside other applications. Each route needs to be evaluated according to its actual account, settings, terms, and data flow.


An internally built interface also needs scrutiny. If it sends requests to an external model API, the company still needs to understand and approve that transfer.


For an organization, approving a provider is only the beginning. It also needs to know which products and accounts employees are using, what information passes through them, and which protections apply. That understanding must keep pace as tools, settings, and terms change.


## **Two principles for retaining control**


### **1) Private Deployment**


Private deployment gives organizations a clear path to expanding AI adoption while retaining control over the knowledge that makes it valuable. Models and their supporting workflows operate within the company’s environment, where internal data, prompts, and outputs remain under its own governance.


This is the approach we take at Datasaur: deploy AI privately within your environment so your teams can put proprietary knowledge to work without sending it to an external model provider. The organization controls access, retention, and how that knowledge is used.


That boundary also accounts for human error. Employee training matters, but even the most careful people make mistakes. An accidental paste, the wrong attachment, or a moment of misplaced confidence can disclose proprietary information. Once a prompt has been sent to an external service, recognizing the mistake does not undo the transfer.


A secured private environment provides protection beyond individual judgment. With models, data flows, and access properly contained, those mistakes can remain within a boundary the organization controls. Teams have room to experiment, learn, and improve without every click of “send” becoming a decision about whether company knowledge should leave the business.


This creates room for more meaningful innovation, because experimentation and iteration become rapid. Employees can work with the actual processes, decision criteria, and institutional expertise that differentiate the company. The knowledge that makes AI useful can stay within the environment where its value belongs.


### **2) Own the Model and Harness**


An enterprise AI solution should evolve according to the organization’s priorities. When the business depends on a provider’s technology, changes to model versions, availability, terms, or pricing can force it to adapt on someone else’s schedule. A workflow that meets the company’s requirements today may become more expensive, operate differently, or fall under different data-handling terms tomorrow.


The deeper that dependency becomes, the harder it can be to respond. If prompts, integrations, evaluations, and application logic are tied to one provider, changing course can mean rebuilding work the organization has already invested in.


Ownership provides greater directional stability. The organization controls the harness surrounding the model: the application logic, prompts, retrieval, evaluations, and workflows that determine how the system operates. It can evaluate alternative models while preserving the knowledge and processes its teams have developed.


This is the autonomy Datasaur is built to support. Your organization owns and controls the system around the model. With privately deployed models, it can retain a working version, test upgrades against its requirements, and introduce changes when ready.


The technology will continue to change. Ownership gives your organization control over how those changes reach the business, so improvements follow your roadmap and serve your goals.


## **From AI Uncertainty to Enterprise Innovation**


A useful enterprise AI system reflects more than the capabilities of its underlying model. It also reflects the context, instructions, examples, and judgment supplied by the organization using it.


Those contributions deserve an explicit ownership strategy.


Before expanding AI use, a business should be able to explain where that knowledge goes, which rules govern its use, and how the company retains control as tools and providers change.


When your AI solution is privately owned by your organization – you have clarity.


Clarity about where your knowledge lives, who can access it, and whose future it is helping build.


Clarity about what changes, when it changes, and who decides.


Your teams can move forward knowing that every workflow refined, every lesson captured, and every improvement made builds on a foundation that remains their own.


The technology will keep moving. Now you can set sail on a ship you built.
